subject: law
title: Unit 1 - Introduction to Law
intro: Learn to separate legal rules, moral arguments, criminal punishment and civil remedies through the two supplied classroom case studies.

blocks.text: The introductory slides define law as rules made and enforced by government to regulate conduct in society. Law also expresses values: a legal system is expected to protect rights, promote fairness, resolve conflict and provide order. These purposes can pull in different directions.

A moral judgement asks whether conduct is right or wrong. A legal judgement asks how a legal rule applies. The slides explicitly invite examples of legal but immoral conduct and morally defensible but unlawful conduct; they do not treat the two categories as identical.
State the rule, identify the conduct, and explain the reasoning. Moral approval alone does not demonstrate legality.

lessons.title: The shipwreck case: facts, rule and argument

source_refs.locator: The Shipwrecked Sailors, factual account and questions

blocks.text: In the supplied hypothetical, three survivors have no food or equipment. They draw lots after prolonged starvation; the selected sailor withdraws consent, but the other two deliberately kill him. They are later rescued and tried under a rule making deliberate killing murder. Treat this as the classroom scenario as written, rather than a verified account of a historical judgment.

source_refs.locator: The Shipwrecked Sailors, factual account and questions

blocks.text: The prosecution can connect the deliberate killing to the stated rule. A defence argument can emphasise extreme necessity and the conditions of survival. The worksheet then asks separately about conviction, punishment, the purposes of punishment and morality. It supplies questions, not an authoritative verdict or a necessity defence.

lessons.title: One event can lead to two legal proceedings

blocks.text: In the accident worksheet, the state prosecutes the driver for drunk driving. Separately, the injured driver sues for repair costs, medical bills and lost work. The first proceeding concerns a crime; the second concerns a private claim for compensation. The same event supplies facts for both.

The worksheet distinguishes guilty/not guilty in the criminal case from liable/not liable in the civil case. Its criminal branch ends in a sentence, while its civil branch ends in a remedy. The exact penalties in the story are scenario details, not universal sentencing rules.

values: Is the defendant liable for the claimed harm?

images.alt: Diagram following the same car crash into a criminal trial and a civil trial
images.caption: Trace each branch independently; shared facts do not make the two proceedings identical.

flashcards.back: Law concerns government-made and enforced rules; morality concerns judgements of right and wrong. The slides explain why they overlap without being identical.

flashcards.front: Who brings the criminal case in the accident story?
flashcards.back: The state prosecutes the driver for violating the drunk-driving law.

flashcards.front: What is the civil remedy in the accident story?
flashcards.back: Money to compensate the injured driver for medical bills and repairs.

flashcards.front: What does the sailors worksheet actually establish?
flashcards.back: It supplies a hypothetical rule and disputed facts, then asks for arguments. It does not supply an official verdict.

questions.prompt: Which claim belongs to the civil branch of the accident story?
options: The state seeks punishment for drunk driving
The injured driver seeks reimbursement for repairs
The legislature votes on a new offence
questions.explanation: The private claimant asks for compensation. The state prosecution is the criminal branch.

questions.prompt: Why must the sailors’ survival argument be distinguished from a legal conclusion?
options: Any moral argument changes the written rule
The worksheet asks for arguments but supplies no authoritative decision
The worksheet states an automatic acquittal
questions.explanation: Necessity is an argument to analyse here; the handout does not announce a legal exception or judgment.

source_refs.locator: The Shipwrecked Sailors, factual account and questions

questions.prompt: Which distinction is made by the introduction?
options: Only criminal rules count as law
Legal and moral are always identical
An act may be legal yet judged immoral
questions.explanation: The values slide explicitly separates legal and moral judgements.

questions.prompt: Can the same accident produce both criminal and civil proceedings in the worksheet?
options: Yes, because punishment and compensation address different questions
No, one proceeding automatically replaces the other
Only if neither person was injured
questions.explanation: The diagram deliberately follows one event into two distinct cases.
